title: Scope Is the Boundary of What You Are Paying For
summary: Marco and Quincy define scope as the owner's written boundary: the work breakdown structure, cost codes that carry it into the accounts, the schedule of values that decides how fast you pay, and the exclusions that are really future change orders. Change control keeps every change deliberate.
body:
Scope is the written boundary of what you are paying for. If the boundary is complete, priced and controlled, the project's cost can only move for reasons you choose; if it has gaps, the contractor will fill them, at a price you did not compete.

Recall

Q. What is apparent authority?

A. Authority a third party may rely on because the principal's own conduct reasonably led them to believe the agent held it.

Q. What is debt yield?

A. Net operating income divided by the loan amount, a lender's measure of how much income the loan earns regardless of interest rate or amortisation.

Q. Why are condo buyer deposits usually held in trust or escrow?

A. Because they are the buyers' money, at risk if the project fails; trust or escrow protects them until conditions for release, such as completion or insurance, are met. The rules vary by jurisdiction.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, last week we built the owner's control system: who decides, how they report, and where decisions are recorded. This week we decide what is being controlled. The single largest source of cost growth on most projects is not price inflation or bad luck. It is scope that was never fully defined, so that the contract sum covered less than everyone thought. Quincy, our cost and quantity surveyor, joins Marco this week because scope and money are the same document seen from two sides.

The work breakdown structure: the whole project, in pieces

In plain English, a work breakdown structure is the project broken down into smaller and smaller pieces until each piece is small enough to price, assign and check.

The professional term is the work breakdown structure (WBS): a hierarchy of deliverables, not activities. Its governing rule is the 100 percent rule: the pieces at each level add up to exactly the whole of the level above, with nothing missing and nothing counted twice. If a piece of work is not in the WBS, nobody is responsible for it, and it will appear later as a change.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 60-unit rental building with a total project budget of 20,000,000 dollars. Level one: 1 land and acquisition, 2 soft costs, 3 site works, 4 substructure, 5 superstructure, 6 envelope, 7 interiors, 8 mechanical, electrical and plumbing, 9 external works, 10 finance costs, 11 contingency. Under 6 envelope, level two: 6.1 exterior walls, 6.2 windows and doors, 6.3 roofing, 6.4 balconies and railings. Under 6.2, level three: 6.2.1 window supply, 6.2.2 window installation, 6.2.3 sealants and flashings at window openings. Notice the last line. Flashings at openings are where trades meet, and they are the classic gap: the window installer thinks the wall contractor does them, and the wall contractor thinks the window installer does.

Cost codes: the WBS in the accounts

In plain English, a cost code is the WBS number written on every invoice, budget line and change, so money can be traced back to the piece of work it bought.

Use the same structure for budget, commitments, invoices, changes and forecasts. Then the monthly report can say, for code 6.2: budget 1,200,000 dollars, committed 1,150,000, changes 40,000, forecast 1,190,000. Without a shared code, the accountant's ledger and the project manager's budget become two different stories, and reconciling them takes a week every month. Choose the codes before you tender, so the contractor's breakdown, your budget and your accounts all speak one language.

The schedule of values: how the contract sum is cut up for payment

In plain English, the schedule of values is the contractor's list of how much of the contract sum belongs to each part of the work, used to calculate each monthly payment.

It matters because you pay against it. If the schedule of values puts too much money in the early items, you pay for work in advance of its real value. That is front-loading, and it is the most common way an owner ends up holding too little money when a contractor fails.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A 15,000,000 dollar construction contract. The contractor's schedule of values lists mobilisation at 600,000 dollars and site works at 1,500,000 dollars. Quincy's own estimate values mobilisation at 150,000 and site works at 1,100,000. Together the early items are overvalued by 850,000 dollars. If the contractor completes those items in the first three months and bills them in full, you have paid 850,000 dollars ahead of value. Should he then fail, the money left in the contract may not finish the building. The control is to review the schedule of values against an independent estimate before the first payment and refuse a breakdown that does not match the value of the work.

Say that out loud now.

The WBS defines the work. The cost codes trace the money. The schedule of values decides how fast I pay, and I check it before the first payment.

Exclusions, assumptions and change control

Every bid and every contract has a list of exclusions: things the price does not include. Read them as a list of future change orders. "Excludes rock removal." "Excludes permits and fees." "Excludes winter heating." Each is either something you will carry in your own budget, something you will move into the contract before signing, or a risk you accept knowingly. An exclusion you never read is a cost you never budgeted.

Assumptions are the mirror image: conditions the price relies on, such as "assumes normal soil" or "assumes continuous access." When an assumption fails, the contractor will argue the price changes with it.

Change control is the process that protects the defined scope once the contract is signed: every proposed change is identified, described, priced, checked against budget and schedule, approved under the authority matrix, and recorded, before the work is done wherever possible. Change control does not stop change. It makes change deliberate.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: cost codes that separate land, building, equipment and soft costs help support how costs are classified for tax purposes; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: a complete scope reduces the gaps that turn into disputes over who was responsible for what. Banking: lenders fund against a budget; a schedule of values that matches it keeps draws aligned with value. Governance: change control is the authority matrix in action; every change passes through it. Estate: a coded, documented project can be handed to someone else to finish. Exit: a buyer's due diligence will test the scope against what was built; clean records make the asset easier to sell or refinance.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor or cost consultant, on the WBS, cost codes and schedule of values; lawyer, on the exclusions and change provisions in the contract.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the scope gap: work that falls between two packages or outside all of them, discovered after the contracts are signed, when it can only be bought without competition. The control is a WBS built to the 100 percent rule, a responsibility check of every interface between packages, and a line-by-line read of exclusions before award.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares bids on the bottom line. The lowest bid is often the one with the most exclusions. Compare bids on scope first, line by line, and only then on price.

Callback

In Week 13, Sage built the sources and uses and the cost categories of the pro forma. The WBS is that pro forma taken down to the level where work gets done. If the pro forma's lines and the WBS's codes match, every change on site can be traced back to the return it affects.

Recap

The WBS breaks the project into deliverables that add up to exactly the whole. Cost codes carry that structure into the budget and the accounts. The schedule of values decides how fast you pay and must be checked for front-loading. Exclusions are future changes; read them. Change control makes every change deliberate.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse and a design change nobody re-checked.
checklist: My WBS follows the 100 percent rule at every level.
Budget, commitments, invoices, changes and forecasts all use the same cost codes.
Every interface between trade packages has a named responsible party.
I read every exclusion and assumption before award and decide how each is carried.
Quincy has checked the schedule of values against an independent estimate before the first payment.
Front-loaded items are corrected before the contract is signed.
Every change passes through change control and the authority matrix before the work is done.
head: Field checklist
speak: Scope is the boundary of what I am paying for. I build a work breakdown structure: the project broken into deliverables that add up to exactly the whole, with nothing missing and nothing counted twice. Every invoice, budget line and change carries the same cost code, so money traces back to the work it bought. The contractor's schedule of values cuts the contract sum up for payment, and I check it against an independent estimate before the first payment, because front-loading means I pay ahead of value and hold too little if the contractor fails. Exclusions in a bid are future change orders, so I read every one and decide whether to carry it, move it into the contract or accept it. Assumptions are conditions the price relies on. And change control makes every change deliberate: identified, priced, checked against budget and schedule, approved under the authority matrix, and recorded before the work is done.
terms: Work breakdown structure (WBS) — a hierarchy that divides a project into deliverables, where each level adds up to exactly the whole of the level above.
Schedule of values — the contractor's breakdown of the contract sum by part of the work, used to calculate progress payments.
Exclusion — an item a bid or contract expressly does not include in its price.

hostile.q: My schedule of values is how we always price. Why are you holding up the first payment over it?
hostile.a: Because I pay against it every month, and on our estimate the mobilisation and site works lines are about 850,000 dollars above the value of that work. I am not asking you to cut your contract sum, only to move that money into the later lines where the work is. Send me a revised breakdown by Friday and the first payment goes through on time.

title: Hyatt Regency 1981: A Change Nobody Re-Checked
summary: Two suspended walkways at the Hyatt Regency in Kansas City fell on 17 July 1981, killing 114 people, after a change from continuous hanger rods to two offset rods doubled the load on one connection. Ford and Cole take it through seven steps and find a change control gap. Rule 49 routes every design change to the designer responsible.
body:
On 17 July 1981, two suspended walkways fell in the atrium of the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City, Missouri, and 114 people died. The cause was a change to one connection that looked like a detailing convenience and doubled the load on it.

Recall

Q. What is the 100 percent rule in a work breakdown structure?

A. The pieces at each level add up to exactly the whole of the level above, with nothing missing and nothing counted twice.

Q. What does Rule 48 say?

A. No change to structure, use or load is approved by the person who profits from it; it goes to the engineer of record in writing, and the owner may refuse the cost but never overrule the safety answer.

Q. What is a lender's monitor?

A. An independent engineer, cost consultant or quantity surveyor hired by the lender to verify progress, cost and changes during construction.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this week is about change control, and no case teaches it more clearly. The change at the centre of the Hyatt Regency collapse was small on paper, proposed for practical reasons, and passed through a review process that existed but did not work. Cole joins Ford because the case also ended in professional discipline, and the legal consequences followed directly from who approved what. The facts below follow the widely reported findings of the federal investigation and the professional licensing proceedings; read the primary sources before you cite any detail.

Step 1: Timeline

The hotel opened in 1980. Its atrium had walkways crossing it at the second, third and fourth floors; the fourth-floor walkway hung directly above the second-floor walkway, both suspended from the roof structure by steel hanger rods. During construction, in 1979, part of the atrium roof had collapsed, a reported event that should have prompted a wider review of the atrium's structure. On the evening of 17 July 1981, during a crowded event in the atrium, the fourth-floor and second-floor walkways fell. 114 people died and more than 200 were injured. A federal investigation by the National Bureau of Standards examined the connections. The engineers responsible were later found guilty of professional misconduct by the state licensing board and lost their licences.

Step 2: Key decisions

The original design showed one set of continuous rods running from the roof through the fourth-floor walkway's box beams and on down to the second-floor walkway, with nuts carrying each walkway. During shop drawing development, the steel fabricator proposed replacing each continuous rod with two shorter rods: one from the roof to the fourth-floor beam, and a second from the fourth-floor beam down to the second-floor walkway. The change made fabrication and erection easier. The engineering firm's review of the shop drawings did not catch what the change did to the load path. The shop drawings were stamped, and the walkways were built that way.

Step 3: Assumptions

Each party assumed the other had checked the structural effect. The fabricator assumed the engineer's review of the shop drawings would confirm the connection worked. The engineer's office treated the shop drawing review as checking conformance, not as a redesign. Everyone assumed a change in rod arrangement was a detailing matter. It was not. With two rods, the fourth-floor box beam connection now carried the weight of the fourth-floor walkway and, through it, the weight of the second-floor walkway hanging below: roughly double what that connection was meant to carry. The investigation also reported that even the original continuous-rod detail fell short of the capacity the building code required, which means the design check had failed before the change, and the change made a weak connection far weaker.

Step 4: Incentives

The incentives were ordinary, which is what makes the case dangerous. The fabricator wanted a detail that was easier to build. The schedule wanted shop drawings turned around quickly. The engineer's office had a large volume of submittals and a fee that did not reward slow, deep checks of connections it considered routine. Nobody gained much by asking hard questions about a hanger rod.

Say that out loud now.

A change that is easier to build must still be checked by the person responsible for the design, against the load path, in writing.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

Two were reported. The 1979 atrium roof collapse during construction was a signal that the atrium's structure deserved a fresh, wider review. And workers were reported to have found the walkways bouncy or uncomfortable to use during construction. Neither became a formal trigger for an engineering re-check of the walkway connections. A warning that has no defined route into the change control process tends to become a story people tell, not a decision anyone makes.

Step 6: Point of no return

Physically, once the walkways were erected on the two-rod detail and loaded with a crowd, nothing could save them. In process terms, the point of no return was the stamped shop drawing: the moment a structurally significant change was accepted as a routine submittal, without a recorded analysis by the engineer of record. After that stamp, the change was invisible inside the documents, and every later inspection looked at a detail that appeared approved.

Step 7: Root cause

The technical root cause was a connection carrying about twice its intended load, on a design that was already short of the code requirement. The process root cause was a change control gap: a design change entered through the submittal process, which was built to check conformance, instead of through a change process that required re-analysis and a clear statement of who was responsible for it. Responsibility for the connection's design fell into the space between the fabricator and the engineer, and nobody owned it.

Cole's note: what the stamp means

Cole draws out the legal point. In professional discipline and in liability, the question is often not who had the idea, but who accepted responsibility for it. A stamped shop drawing is evidence that a licensed professional reviewed and accepted a detail. If your contracts and your submittal procedure do not say clearly which changes the engineer must re-analyse, and do not record that he did, you have a document that looks like approval and a responsibility nobody actually discharged. The owner's lesson is to make the contract say it: any substitution or change to a structural connection is a design change, owned and re-analysed by the engineer of record, and recorded as such.

What this means for a small developer

A worked example, hypothetical. Your contractor proposes changing balcony connections from cast-in plates to post-installed anchors to save two weeks. In your change log it must arrive as a design change, not a submittal: the structural engineer re-analyses the connection, states the load and the anchor capacity, and signs; the change is logged with the analysis attached; and inspection checks the as-built anchors against the new design. If the engineer's review fee is 4,000 dollars and the change saves 30,000, you are still ahead, and you have a record.

Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record, on any substitution or change to a structural element or connection.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a design change entering through a back door: a shop drawing, a request for information answer or a site instruction, all built to check or clarify, not to redesign. The control is a rule that any change to a structural element, connection, fire separation or life-safety system is a design change, routed through change control and re-analysed in writing by the designer responsible.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks a stamp on a shop drawing means the engineer has fully checked everything on it. Ask what the review covered, and make the contract define it.

Callback

In Week 48, the Sampoong collapse showed an owner overruling engineers. Hyatt shows the opposite failure: nobody overruled anyone, and the change still went through, because the process treated a redesign as a formality. Rule 48 and Rule 49 together close both doors.

Recap

A change from continuous rods to two offset rods doubled the load on the fourth-floor connection of a design already short of code, the change passed as a shop drawing, and the walkways fell. Rule 49: no design change is accepted until the designer responsible has re-analysed it in writing, and any change to structure or life safety goes through change control, never through a submittal alone.

Next: Quincy, on The Money: what a scope gap costs once the contract is signed.
checklist: My contracts define which changes are design changes requiring re-analysis.
Any substitution to a structural element or connection is re-analysed and signed by the engineer of record.
Shop drawings, RFI answers and site instructions cannot carry a redesign.
I know what the engineer's submittal review covers and what it does not.
Every design change is logged with its analysis attached.
Distress during construction, such as unexpected movement or cracking, triggers a formal engineering review.
Inspections check as-built work against the approved change, not the original drawing.
head: Field checklist
speak: On 17 July 1981, two walkways fell in the atrium of the Hyatt Regency in Kansas City and 114 people died. The original design hung both walkways from one set of continuous rods. During shop drawings, the fabricator proposed two shorter rods, one to the fourth floor and a second from there to the second floor. That was easier to build, but it doubled the load on the fourth-floor connection, which the investigation reported was already short of what the code required. The change passed as a shop drawing review, built to check conformance rather than redesign, and responsibility fell between fabricator and engineer. The engineers later lost their licences. My rule, Rule 49: no design change is accepted until the designer responsible has re-analysed it in writing. Any change to structure or life safety goes through change control and is logged with its analysis, never slipped through a submittal.
terms: Shop drawing — a detailed drawing prepared by a fabricator or subcontractor showing how it will make and install part of the work, submitted for the designer's review.
Load path — the route by which loads travel through a structure's members and connections down to the foundations.
Submittal review — the designer's check that a contractor's submission conforms to the design intent, which is not the same as a full redesign.

hostile.q: It's a shop drawing. Your engineer stamped it. Why are you now asking for a separate design change and a new analysis?
hostile.a: Because the stamp tells me the engineer reviewed the drawing for conformance, and this drawing changes how the connection carries load. Under our contract that makes it a design change, which the engineer of record must re-analyse and sign as such. I have asked him for a written check by Wednesday. If it works, we proceed with the record in the change log. If it does not, we have avoided a problem nobody can fix once it is built.

rule: Rule 49: No design change is accepted until the designer responsible has re-analysed it in writing; any change to structure or life safety goes through change control and is logged with its analysis, never through a submittal alone.

title: What a Scope Gap Costs After the Contract Is Signed
summary: Work left out at tender is bought later without competition, with markup, disruption and time. Quincy prices a hypothetical missing railing package at nearly twice its tender value, shows the cost and exposure of front-loading, and explains how a responsibility matrix and bid levelling catch gaps before award.
body:
A dollar of scope bought at tender is bought in competition. The same dollar bought after award is bought from one supplier, with markup, time and leverage on his side. The gap between those two prices is what a poor scope costs.

Recall

Q. What is front-loading in a schedule of values?

A. Putting more of the contract sum into early items than their real value, so the owner pays ahead of work done.

Q. What does Rule 49 say?

A. No design change is accepted until the designer responsible has re-analysed it in writing; any change to structure or life safety goes through change control and is logged with its analysis.

Q. What is the time-related cost of a project?

A. The cost it incurs for every day or month it stays open: finance carry, monthly overheads and deferred net operating income.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the pro forma treats construction cost as one number. In reality it is two: the price you agreed, and the price of everything you forgot to agree. The second number is almost always paid at a premium. Knowing how large that premium is, and where it comes from, is the reason a good owner spends real money and time on scope before he tenders.

Why post-award scope costs more

In plain English: once the contract is signed, the contractor is the only one who can do the extra work without disruption, so he sets the price.

The professional framing has four parts. First, loss of competition: there is no second bidder. Second, markup: the change carries the contractor's overhead and profit, often on top of a subcontractor's own overhead and profit; the percentages are commercial practice set in the contract or negotiated, not standards. Third, disruption: work added mid-stream can interrupt other work, and the contractor will price that. Fourth, time: if the change is on the critical path, it adds time-related cost, which you met in Week 48.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A balcony railing package was left out of the tender documents. Had it been tendered, Quincy estimates three bids around 200,000 dollars. Bought as a change after award, the price is built like this: the subcontractor's cost 200,000 dollars plus his 10 percent overhead and profit, 220,000; the main contractor's 5 percent on the subcontract, 11,000; bond and insurance at about 1.5 percent, roughly 3,500; disruption to the scaffold sequence, 15,000. Total about 249,500 dollars. If the late order also adds two weeks on the critical path at 70,000 dollars a week of time-related cost, the real cost is about 389,500 dollars. The scope gap did not cost 200,000. It cost nearly twice that.

Front-loading and the cost of paying early

Scope and the schedule of values interact. A front-loaded schedule of values does not change the contract sum, but it changes when you pay, and money paid early has a cost.

A second worked example, hypothetical. On a 15,000,000 dollar contract, early lines are overvalued by 850,000 dollars, paid on average twelve months ahead of when the work's true value would have been earned. If the money is drawn on a construction loan at 8 percent, the interest cost of paying early is roughly 850,000 times 8 percent, about 68,000 dollars. That is the small cost. The large one is exposure: if the contractor fails in month 10, you have paid 850,000 dollars for work not yet in place, and the replacement contractor will want paying again for it. Retainage, the share of each payment held back until completion, softens that exposure but does not remove it.

Say that out loud now.

A scope gap is bought without competition, with markup, disruption and time on top. It can cost twice its tender value.

How the best do it

Disciplined owners and their cost consultants build a responsibility matrix before tender: a table of every interface between trade packages, such as window to wall, roof to parapet, firestopping at service penetrations, and temporary protection, with one named package responsible for each. Then they level the bids: they lay each bidder's inclusions and exclusions side by side, line by line, and put a price on every gap before comparing totals. A small developer can copy both with a spreadsheet and two afternoons with the cost consultant, and the first scope gap they catch usually pays for the whole exercise.

What scope discipline does to return

Put the numbers together. On a 20,000,000 dollar project, suppose an owner with weak scope ends up with change orders of 8 percent of the construction contract, and an owner with strong scope holds them to 3 percent; both ranges are illustrative, not benchmarks. On a 15,000,000 dollar contract, that is 1,200,000 dollars against 450,000, a difference of 750,000 dollars. Against 6,000,000 dollars of equity, 750,000 dollars is 12.5 percent of the equity, and it comes out of the equity first, because contingency and equity are spent before the lender's money. That one variable can move the equity multiple more than a good rent assumption.

Run the equity multiple, the total cash returned divided by the equity invested, on a simple hypothetical. Suppose the project returns 9,000,000 dollars to equity at sale with strong scope. Equity invested is 6,000,000 dollars, so the multiple is 1.5 times. With weak scope, the extra 750,000 dollars of changes is equity that goes in and earns nothing extra, so 6,750,000 dollars invested returns the same 9,000,000 dollars, a multiple of about 1.33 times. Nothing about the market changed. The rent, the exit cap rate and the loan were identical. Only the owner's discipline before tender moved, and it cut the equity's profit from 3,000,000 dollars to 2,250,000 dollars, a quarter of it gone. That is why experienced investors ask a developer how he controls change orders before they ask about his rent assumptions.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, scope gaps are an uninsured liability that appears in the middle of the project, exactly when your liquidity is most committed. Equity is first in, so an overrun means either a new capital call on you, a guarantee called, or dilution if a partner funds it. A developer with a reputation for clean scopes also pays less for equity and debt over time, because investors and lenders price his overrun risk lower. Scope discipline is therefore a wealth habit, not just a project habit. Conceptual only; a licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor or cost consultant, on the responsibility matrix, bid levelling and pricing of changes.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is comparing bids on totals before comparing them on scope, which rewards the bidder who left the most out. The control is bid levelling against a responsibility matrix, with every gap priced, before any award decision.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sees a change order as a price and negotiates the price. The real cost includes the markup chain, disruption and time. Negotiate the whole, and better still, prevent it at tender. A change order that looks reasonable on its own can still be the most expensive way to buy that work, and the question to ask is always what it would have cost if it had been in the tender documents.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman built tornado charts to show which inputs move a return most. If you ran one on a typical development, change-order growth would sit near the top of the chart, often above construction escalation. Today shows why: it compounds through markup, time and equity, all at once.

Recap

Scope bought after award loses competition and gathers markup, disruption and time, and can cost twice its tender value. Front-loading costs interest and, more seriously, exposure if the contractor fails. A responsibility matrix and bid levelling price the gaps before award, where the money is cheap.

Next: LEX, on The Rules: change clauses, who may order a change, and how Canada and Guyana approach it.
checklist: I build a responsibility matrix for every interface between trade packages before tender.
I level bids line by line, pricing every gap, before comparing totals.
I price changes as the full chain: cost, markup, bond, disruption and time.
I know the contract's markup percentages on changes before award.
I check whether each change is on the critical path before negotiating it.
I count the interest and exposure cost of any front-loading.
I track change orders as a percentage of contract and against the equity they consume.
head: Field checklist
speak: A dollar of scope bought at tender is bought in competition. Bought after award, it loses competition and gathers the subcontractor's markup, the main contractor's markup, bond and insurance, disruption to the sequence and, if it is on the critical path, the project's time-related cost. On a hypothetical railing package worth 200,000 dollars at tender, that chain takes it to about 389,500 dollars. Front-loading the schedule of values costs interest on money paid early and, worse, exposure if the contractor fails before the work exists. Overruns come out of equity first, so on a 6,000,000 dollar equity cheque, holding change orders to 3 percent instead of 8 percent of a 15,000,000 dollar contract saves about 750,000 dollars, 12.5 percent of the equity. The best owners build a responsibility matrix of every interface and level bids line by line, pricing every gap before comparing totals.
terms: Markup — the percentage added to a cost for overhead and profit, often applied in layers by subcontractor and main contractor.
Responsibility matrix — a table assigning each interface between trade packages to one named responsible package.
Bid levelling — comparing bids line by line on scope, inclusions and exclusions, pricing every gap before comparing totals.

hostile.q: The railing was never in the documents. Why should my price be anything less than market for a change?
hostile.a: Your price should be fair, and you will be paid for the work. I am asking for the build-up: your subcontractor's quotes, the markup percentages the contract sets for changes, and any disruption you are claiming with the activities affected. I will also check whether it is on the critical path. Send the breakdown and we will settle it quickly, and the scope gap is our lesson to fix at tender next time.

title: The Change Clause: Who Orders, How It Is Priced, When Notice Is Due
summary: LEX explains the four parts of every change clause: the owner's right to change within the general scope, change orders and change directives, the valuation ladder, and notice provisions that can bar a claim. A Two Systems section compares Canada and Guyana conceptually.
body:
The change clause is the most used clause in any construction contract. It decides who may order a change, how the work proceeds before the price is agreed, how the price is set, and what happens if notice is not given in time.

Recall

Q. What is ratification by conduct?

A. Adopting an unauthorised act after the event, most commonly by paying for the work, so that it binds the principal as if authorised.

Q. What is bid levelling?

A. Comparing bids line by line on scope, inclusions and exclusions, and pricing every gap before comparing totals.

Q. What is a conditional sale in a condo pre-sale context?

A. A sale whose closing depends on stated conditions, such as financing or completion, often with deposit release rules; the details are contractual and vary by jurisdiction.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, on most projects you will sign dozens or hundreds of changes. The change clause decides whether each one is a calm administrative step or the start of a claim. This lesson teaches the concepts every change clause contains. It is not a jurisdictional conclusion; contracts and local law differ, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it, and have your lawyer read the actual clause.

The owner's right to change

In plain English: a construction contract gives the owner the right to change the work, within limits, without making a new contract each time.

Without that right, every change would need the contractor's agreement, and the contractor could refuse or name any price. Standard forms solve this by giving the owner a unilateral right to order changes within the general scope of the contract, and requiring the contractor to carry them out, with a mechanism to adjust price and time. The phrase "within the general scope" matters. A change so large or different that it creates a fundamentally different project may fall outside the clause. In United States law this is discussed under the idea of a cardinal change, and other systems reach similar results by different routes; the boundaries are a matter for local law and the contract's words.

Change order and change directive

Most modern forms use two instruments. A change order is a written agreement, signed by owner and contractor, recording a change and its agreed effect on price and time. A change directive, called a construction change directive in some American forms, is a written instruction from the owner to proceed with a change before price and time are agreed, with the adjustment to be settled later under a stated method. International forms often use the word variation for the same idea, issued by the engineer administering the contract.

The directive is your tool for the situation in last week's meeting: the work must proceed now, and the price can wait. Its protection lies in its terms: it should say the work proceeds, the valuation method that applies, and that the contractor must keep records of actual cost.

Say that out loud now.

A change order is agreed price and time. A change directive is go now, price later, by a method we already agreed.

Valuation, notice and time bars

The clause sets how changes are valued, usually in a ladder: first, unit rates already in the contract; then rates derived from them; then an agreed lump sum; and if none of these, actual cost plus a stated markup. A worked example, hypothetical: the contract contains a unit rate of 90 dollars a cubic metre for excavation. A change adds 1,000 cubic metres of similar work. The value is 90,000 dollars, by the contract's own rate, with little room for argument. If the added work is rock, which the rates do not cover, the parties move down the ladder to an agreed price or cost plus markup, and records of actual cost become essential.

Most clauses also require notice. A contractor who believes an instruction is a change must say so in writing within a stated period, often before proceeding. Some contracts make that notice a condition precedent, meaning that if it is not given in time, the right to more money or time is lost; such provisions are often called time bars. Courts in different places enforce time bars with different strictness, and some soften them for fairness; that is a question for your lawyer on your contract. The owner's practical lesson is two-sided: insist on timely notice, and give your own notices on time.

Owners have notice duties too. Many forms require the owner to respond to a claimed change, or to a request for information, within a stated time, and silence can be treated as acceptance or can itself create a delay claim. Put your own response periods in the decision log as dates needed, exactly as you did in Week 48, so the contract's clock and your log run together.

A second worked example, hypothetical. The contract requires notice of a claimed change within 14 days of the instruction. The contractor proceeds with extra firestopping on day 3 and first mentions it in a payment application on day 60. Under a strictly enforced time bar, the claim may fail. Under a softer approach, it may survive but with the burden on the contractor to prove the cost. Either way, the record you keep of when the instruction was given decides the argument. The owner should therefore log every instruction with its date and the person who gave it, so the notice clock can be measured by facts rather than memory.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

A conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source before relying on any point. In Canada, outside Quebec, construction contracts sit in a common-law system, and many private projects use standard forms prepared by the Canadian Construction Documents Committee, whose stipulated-price contract provides for both change orders and change directives [unverified — confirm independently]. Provincial statutes on construction liens, holdbacks and, in some provinces, prompt payment shape how changed work is paid and secured, and they differ province by province [unverified — confirm independently]. Quebec uses a civil code, which approaches contract terms from a different starting point.

Guyana's legal system is also founded on English common law, so concepts such as freedom of contract, notice clauses and the interpretation of standard forms will be familiar in outline [unverified — confirm independently]. Public works are governed by national procurement legislation and oversight bodies, and internationally funded projects in the region commonly use FIDIC forms, in which the engineer issues variations [unverified — confirm independently]. The practical difference for an owner is less about doctrine than about which standard form, which statutes on payment and security, and which dispute route apply; establish all three with local counsel before you sign.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on the change, valuation, notice and time-bar provisions of the specific contract and the governing law.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an owner who lets changes proceed on verbal instructions and then relies on a time bar he himself undermined by his conduct. The control is to use the instruments the contract provides, change order or change directive, every time, and to keep a dated record of every instruction and notice.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks the change clause is about price. It is first about authority and time: who may order, how fast notice must be given, and how the work proceeds before price is settled.

Callback

In Week 20, LEX taught conditions and conditions precedent in contract formation. A notice requirement written as a condition precedent is that same idea, used in the middle of a project: the right to payment exists only if the condition, timely notice, is met.

Recap

The owner has a right to order changes within the general scope. A change order records agreed price and time; a change directive orders work to proceed first. Valuation follows a ladder from contract rates to cost plus markup. Notice provisions, sometimes time bars, decide whether claims survive. Canada and Guyana both start from common law, with different forms and statutes.

Next: Quincy, on The Numbers: pricing a change step by step and updating the change log.
checklist: I know what my contract allows me to change, and what might fall outside its general scope.
I use a signed change order when price and time are agreed.
I use a written change directive, with a stated valuation method, when work must proceed first.
I know the contract's valuation ladder and markup percentages.
I know the notice periods and whether they are drafted as conditions precedent.
I keep a dated record of every instruction and every notice, given and received.
My lawyer has read the change clause and the governing law before award.
head: Field checklist
speak: The change clause is the most used clause in a construction contract. It gives the owner the right to order changes within the general scope, without a new contract each time, and requires the contractor to carry them out. A change order records an agreed change in price and time, signed by both. A change directive tells the contractor to proceed now, with the price settled later by a method the contract already states, and with actual cost records kept. Valuation follows a ladder: contract unit rates, rates derived from them, an agreed lump sum, then actual cost plus markup. Most clauses require written notice within a stated period, and some make it a condition precedent, a time bar, though courts enforce those with different strictness. Canada and Guyana both start from common law, but the forms and payment statutes differ, so I confirm them with local counsel.
terms: Change directive — a written instruction from the owner to proceed with a change before price and time are agreed, valued later by a stated method.
Time bar — a notice provision under which a claim for money or time is lost if notice is not given within the stated period.
Cardinal change — in United States law, a change so fundamental that it falls outside the contract's change clause altogether.

hostile.q: Your directive says to proceed but sets no price. How do I know I will be paid fairly?
hostile.a: Because the contract already says how a directive is valued: first by the contract's unit rates, then by agreement, and failing that by your actual cost plus the contract's markup. Keep daily records of labour, plant and materials on this work, signed by our representative each day, and the valuation will rest on facts we have both seen. If we cannot agree, the contract's dispute process applies, but on records like that we rarely need it.

title: Pricing a Change, Step by Step
summary: Quincy builds a hypothetical change from quantities to direct cost, markups, bond and insurance, and checks whether float absorbs the time. He compares the build-up with the contractor's quote, settles the difference on quantity, then records the change in the log and updates contingency against work remaining.
body:
A change is priced in five layers and recorded in two places. Build the price step by step, compare it with the contractor's quote, then update the change log and the contingency so you always know what is left.

Recall

Q. What is the valuation ladder in a typical change clause?

A. Contract unit rates first, then rates derived from them, then an agreed lump sum, and failing those, actual cost plus a stated markup.

Q. What does a responsibility matrix do?

A. It assigns each interface between trade packages to one named responsible package, so no work falls between them.

Q. What is the in-balance test?

A. Undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity must cover the full cost to complete; any shortfall is deposited before the next draw.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a change order arrives as a single number on a cover sheet. Behind it is a stack of assumptions about quantities, hours, rates and markups. If you cannot rebuild that stack yourself, you are negotiating against someone else's arithmetic. Today we build one change from the ground up and then carry it into the project's records. All figures are hypothetical round numbers.

The change

The architect issues a revision upgrading the corridor walls on four residential floors from a single layer of gypsum board to a two-layer, higher acoustic rating assembly, after a review of sound transmission between units. The contractor quotes 96,000 dollars and one week. You will check it.

Step 1: Quantities

Quincy measures the drawings. Corridor wall length is 120 metres per floor, at a height of 2.7 metres, with both faces affected on the unit side only, so one face. Area per floor: 120 times 2.7 is 324 square metres. Four floors: 324 times 4 is 1,296 square metres. Allow 10 percent for waste and cutting: 1,296 times 1.1 is about 1,426 square metres of additional board.

Step 2: Direct cost

Materials: the additional board, screws, acoustic sealant and finishing at a hypothetical 14 dollars a square metre on the 1,426 square metres: 1,426 times 14 is 19,964, call it 20,000 dollars. Labour: the crew installs and finishes the extra layer at 0.5 labour hours per square metre on the 1,296 square metres actually installed, which is 648 hours. At an all-in labour rate of 60 dollars an hour, that is 38,880 dollars. Equipment and small tools: 2,000 dollars. Direct cost: 20,000 plus 38,880 plus 2,000 is 60,880 dollars.

Step 3: Markup layers

The contract, as commercial practice negotiated at award, allows the subcontractor 10 percent for overhead and profit on his own work, and the main contractor 5 percent on subcontracted work. Subcontractor: 60,880 times 1.10 is 66,968 dollars. Main contractor: 66,968 times 1.05 is 70,316 dollars. Bond and insurance at 1.5 percent: 70,316 times 0.015 is about 1,055, giving 71,371 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Quantity, direct cost, subcontractor markup, contractor markup, bond and insurance: about 71,400 dollars before any time.

Step 4: Time

Is the change on the critical path? The schedule shows corridor finishes on floors two to five have eight working days of float before they delay flooring and doors. The added layer takes the drywall crew five extra working days. Five is less than eight, so the change does not move completion, and no time-related cost is due. Had the float been only two days, three days would have pushed completion, and at a hypothetical 14,000 dollars a working day of time-related cost, the change would carry another 42,000 dollars and an extension of time.

Step 5: Compare and negotiate

Your build-up is about 71,400 dollars with no time. The contractor's quote is 96,000 dollars and one week. The gap is 24,600 dollars, about 34 percent above your figure. Ask for his build-up and look in three places: a higher quantity, perhaps both wall faces instead of one; a higher labour productivity assumption; or a time charge you have shown is not due because float absorbs it. Suppose his build-up shows both faces. Check the architect's revision; it calls for the unit side only. He corrects the quantity and agrees 72,500 dollars, no time. The change order is signed at that figure.

Step 6: Record it in two places

First, the change log. Change 23: corridor acoustic upgrade, floors two to five, cost code 7.1.2 interior partitions, requested by the owner through the architect, cause category owner design improvement, approved by the owner's representative under the matrix because it is between 25,000 and 100,000 dollars, price 72,500 dollars, time nil, signed date recorded. Cumulative approved changes before this one: 310,000 dollars. After: 382,500 dollars. On a 15,000,000 dollar contract, that is 2.55 percent, which has now passed a 2 percent cap on owner changes; under the rule you set in Week 48, every further owner change needs your written approval and a named funding source.

Second, the contingency. Owner's contingency started at 1,000,000 dollars. Before this change, 380,000 dollars had been drawn for changes and unforeseen items. After: 452,500 dollars drawn, 547,500 dollars remaining, 54.75 percent of the original. The project is 50 percent complete, so 50 percent of the work remains against 54.75 percent of contingency. You are slightly ahead of the burn rule, but only slightly, and the report should say so.

A second, quicker example

A deletion. You remove a decorative feature wall from the lobby, valued in the contract's schedule of values at 40,000 dollars. A deletion is not simply a 40,000 dollar credit. Ask what has already been bought: if 12,000 dollars of materials are delivered and cannot be returned, and the contractor has incurred 3,000 dollars of design coordination, the fair credit is 40,000 less 12,000 less 3,000, which is 25,000 dollars, and the delivered materials become yours. Agree the credit and ownership of the materials in the change order, or you will argue about both later.

Why the build-up is worth the effort

Look at what the exercise bought. One hour of measurement and arithmetic moved the price by 23,500 dollars and removed a week that was never due. Across a project with 60 or 80 changes, the same discipline typically matters more than any single negotiation, because contractors learn quickly which owners check and which do not. An owner who returns every quote with a written build-up of his own receives sharper first quotes on the next change. There is also a record benefit. If a change is ever disputed, your build-up, dated and filed with the change, shows the basis on which you agreed the price, which is far stronger than a signature on a cover sheet. Keep a simple template: quantities, direct cost lines, the contract's markup layers, bond and insurance, time and float, the contractor's figure, the agreed figure, and the reason for any difference.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor or cost consultant, on quantities and valuation of significant changes.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is approving changes one at a time without seeing their running total against the cap and the contingency. The control is to update the change log and the contingency position with every signed change, and to report both every month.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner haggles over the markup percentage and never checks the quantity. Quantity errors are usually larger than markup arguments, and they are facts, not opinions.

Callback

In Week 48, Nadia reverse engineered a final cost report and found that unlabelled changes could not be attributed. Today's change log entry, with cause, code, requester and authority, is exactly the record that makes that analysis possible at the end of the job.

Recap

Price a change in layers: quantity, direct cost, markups, bond and insurance, then time only if float is exhausted. Compare your build-up with the quote and find the difference in quantity, productivity or time. Record it in the change log with code, cause and authority, and update the contingency against work remaining.

Next: Marco, on The Room: the scope gap nobody owns, and the meeting to settle it.
checklist: I measure the change's quantities from the revision myself or through my cost consultant.
I build direct cost from materials, labour hours and rates, and equipment.
I apply the contract's markup layers in order, plus bond and insurance.
I charge time only if the change exhausts the float on its path.
I compare my build-up with the quote and find the difference in quantity, productivity or time.
I record each change with cost code, cause, requester, authority, price and time.
I update cumulative changes against the cap and contingency against work remaining with every signed change.
I value deletions net of materials already bought and agree who owns them.
head: Field checklist
speak: I price a change in layers. First, quantities from the revision: here, 1,296 square metres of extra board plus 10 percent waste. Second, direct cost: materials about 20,000 dollars, 648 labour hours at 60 dollars, 38,880 dollars, and 2,000 dollars of equipment, 60,880 dollars. Third, the contract's markups: 10 percent for the subcontractor, 5 percent for the main contractor, then 1.5 percent bond and insurance, about 71,400 dollars. Fourth, time: the work takes five days and the path has eight days of float, so no time is due. The contractor quoted 96,000 dollars and a week, because he measured both wall faces; corrected, we agree 72,500 dollars and no time. Then I record it: code, cause, requester, authority, price and time, and I update the totals. Cumulative owner changes now pass my 2 percent cap, and contingency remaining is just above work remaining.
terms: Direct cost — the materials, labour and equipment cost of performing work, before overhead, profit, bond and insurance.
Productivity rate — the labour hours needed per unit of work, such as hours per square metre.
Deletion credit — the reduction in contract sum for removed work, net of costs already incurred.

hostile.q: Your quantity surveyor cut my quote by 24,000 dollars. Are you accusing me of padding it?
hostile.a: No. Your build-up measured both faces of the corridor walls, and the architect's revision only changes the unit side, so the quantity was double. On the corrected quantity, at your own rates and the contract's markups, the figure is about 72,500 dollars. If you think the productivity rate or the rates are wrong, show me the basis and I will look at it today.

title: The Scope Gap Nobody Owns
summary: A failed fire separation inspection turns into an argument between two subcontractors, each certain the firestopping is the other's job. Marco shows how to keep life-safety work moving with a directive without prejudice, decide cost on the documents, and use silence to hear what each contract says.
body:
A scope gap arrives as an argument between two of your contractors, each certain the work belongs to the other. Your job in the room is not to decide who is right first. It is to keep the work moving, protect the record, and find out whose documents actually say what.

Recall

Q. What is a deletion credit?

A. The reduction in the contract sum for removed work, net of costs already incurred, such as materials bought and design coordination.

Q. What is the difference between a change order and a change directive?

A. A change order records an agreed change in price and time; a change directive orders the work to proceed first, with price and time settled later by a stated method.

Q. What is Rule 49?

A. No design change is accepted until the designer responsible has re-analysed it in writing; any change to structure or life safety goes through change control and is logged with its analysis.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will rarely face a contractor who simply refuses to do work. You will often face two contractors who each say a piece of work is not theirs. The conversation sounds technical, but it is really about money and precedent. How you handle the first one tells everyone how you will handle the next ten.

The scene

A hypothetical scene. The project uses separate trade contracts managed by your construction manager. At the weekly coordination meeting, the inspector has failed the fire separations at the corridor ceilings because the firestopping around pipe and duct penetrations is incomplete. The mechanical subcontractor says firestopping is the drywall contractor's job. The drywall contractor says penetrations made by others are the responsibility of whoever made them. The construction manager turns to you: "Neither contract is clear. We need a change order to a third party to do it, about 85,000 dollars, or the next inspection slips and we lose two weeks."

The question behind the question

Each person is asking something different. The mechanical subcontractor is asking: will the owner make me do unpaid work? The drywall contractor is asking the same. The construction manager may be asking whether he can avoid admitting that his own scope split left a gap, because writing the trade packages was part of his service. And all of them are asking whether this owner pays to make arguments go away. The fire separation itself is not negotiable: it is life safety, and it must be done properly, inspected and recorded.

The lines to say

"The firestopping gets done and inspected on schedule. That part is not up for discussion. I will not let the sequence slip over who pays."

"So here is the plan. The construction manager issues a change directive today to the drywall contractor, as the trade already on the ceilings, to complete the firestopping, using the approved system, with daily records of labour and materials. That directive is without prejudice to who ultimately bears the cost."

"By Friday, the construction manager sends me the relevant clauses of both trade contracts, the specification section for firestopping, and the responsibility matrix from tender. Then we decide who pays, on the documents."

Say that out loud now.

The work gets done on schedule, without prejudice to who pays. Who pays is decided on the documents by Friday.

The lines never to say

Never say "I'll just pay for it to stop the argument." You will have taught three contractors that ambiguity is profitable. Never say "it's obviously the mechanical contractor's," before reading his contract; you may be wrong, and you have handed the other side an admission. Never say "the inspector is being difficult"; the inspector is enforcing the safety of your building and your future residents. And never accept a firestopping method that differs from the tested, approved system to save time; a change to a fire-rated assembly is a design change under Rule 49.

When to stay silent

When the construction manager says "neither contract is clear," stay silent for a moment and let him continue. If the gap came from his own split of the packages, he will often say so, or show it in how he answers. Silence is also right when the two subcontractors begin arguing with each other: let them set out their positions fully. Each will reveal what his contract says, and you will hear it before you have taken any position.

Holding your state

A failed inspection with a schedule threat creates a sense of urgency that pushes people towards the fastest payment, not the right one. Separate the two clocks in your head. The work clock is urgent and you solve it today with a directive. The money clock is not urgent; a week of reading the documents costs nothing. Name the two clocks out loud in the room, and everyone else's pulse drops with yours.

What the documents usually show

A worked example of the Friday review, hypothetical. The specification's firestopping section requires firestopping of all penetrations, without naming a trade. The drywall contract includes "firestopping at joints and head-of-wall." The mechanical contract includes "sealing of penetrations made by this trade" but not "firestopping." The responsibility matrix from tender has no line for penetration firestopping at all. Conclusion: a genuine scope gap in the trade packages. If the construction manager's agreement made him responsible for defining complete packages, the cost may fall partly on him; that is a question for your lawyer and his contract. Either way, the lesson goes into the next project's matrix: one line, one trade, one responsibility, for every fire-rated penetration.

A second worked example shows the other outcome, also hypothetical. Suppose instead that the mechanical contract says "firestopping of all penetrations made by this trade, using the approved listed system." Then the gap was never real: the mechanical subcontractor priced the work, did not do it, and owes the cost. The drywall contractor, who completed the work under the directive, is paid on his daily records, say 62,000 dollars, and that sum is deducted from the mechanical subcontractor's next payment under his contract's provisions for work done by others. Notice the order of events. Because the directive was without prejudice and the records were kept daily, neither outcome required a dispute. The documents decided it. Had you paid a third party 85,000 dollars in the meeting to make the argument stop, you would have paid 23,000 dollars more than the work cost and left the true responsible party unpaid for nothing.

Professional sign-off required: fire protection engineer or architect, on the firestopping system and its listing; lawyer, on the allocation of cost under the trade and construction management contracts.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting a cost argument delay or degrade life-safety work. The control is to separate the two: direct the work now, using the approved system, without prejudice; decide the cost later, on the documents.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner decides who is to blame in the meeting, from the loudest argument. Blame decided in the room becomes a precedent; blame decided on the documents becomes a record.

Callback

In Week 48, Marco ran the first owner's meeting and refused a verbal yes while still removing the delay with a same-day written direction. Today uses the same move in a three-way dispute: solve the work clock in writing today, and let the money clock run on the documents.

Recap

A scope gap arrives as two contractors pointing at each other. Keep life-safety work moving with a directive, without prejudice, using the approved system. Decide who pays on the contracts, specification and responsibility matrix, not in the room. Stay silent while each side sets out its position, and put the gap into next project's matrix.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap, with a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical change order.
checklist: I separate the work clock from the money clock in every scope dispute.
Life-safety work proceeds by written directive, without prejudice, using the approved system.
I never pay to make an argument go away.
I never assign blame in the room before reading the contracts.
I ask for the clauses, specification section and responsibility matrix within a set date.
I treat any change to a fire-rated assembly as a design change.
I add every gap found to the next project's responsibility matrix.
head: Field checklist
speak: A scope gap usually arrives as two contractors pointing at each other. Here, the corridor firestopping failed inspection and the mechanical and drywall contractors each say it belongs to the other. I separate two clocks. The work clock is urgent: the construction manager issues a directive today to the trade already on the ceilings to complete the firestopping with the approved system, keeping daily records, without prejudice to who pays. The money clock is not urgent: by Friday I want both contracts' clauses, the specification section and the tender responsibility matrix, and we decide who pays on the documents. I never pay to make the argument go away, never assign blame in the room, never criticise the inspector, and never accept a substitute fire-rated system without a design change. I stay silent while each side sets out its position, because their own words tell me what their contracts say.
terms: Without prejudice — wording that lets an action proceed without either party giving up its position on who is ultimately responsible or liable.
Firestopping — tested materials and systems that seal openings and penetrations in fire-rated walls and floors to keep fire and smoke from passing through.
Trade contract — a contract with an individual specialist contractor, often managed by a construction manager acting for the owner.

hostile.q: You're ordering my crew to do firestopping we never priced. Why should we carry that cost?
hostile.a: You may not have to. The directive is without prejudice and says so in writing. It asks you to do the work now because your crew is on the ceilings, to keep daily records, and to be paid on those records. By Friday we will read both trade contracts, the specification and the tender matrix, and decide who bears the cost on the documents. If it lands outside your scope, you are paid in full.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 49 Review: Scope, Changes and the Record
summary: Six questions test the work breakdown structure, front-loading, the cost of scope gaps, change instruments, time and the Hyatt Regency load path. A Red Pen drill finds eight defects in a hypothetical change order, and a two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: define the whole of the work before you buy it, check how fast you pay for it, and make every change after that deliberate, priced, authorised and recorded.

Recall

Q. What is decision latency, and when does it cost money?

A. The time between a decision being needed and being made; it costs the daily time-related cost only when the item is on the critical path and its float is used up.

Q. What does Rule 48 say?

A. No change to structure, use or load is approved by the person who profits from it; it goes to the engineer of record in writing, and the owner may refuse the cost but never overrule the safety answer.

Q. What is a cumulative cap in an authority matrix?

A. A limit on the total value of decisions one person may approve, in addition to the limit on any single decision.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, scope is where cost growth is born. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can sit with a cost consultant, a contractor and a lender's monitor and follow every change on the project. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is the 100 percent rule, and why does it matter?

Answer: The pieces at each level of the work breakdown structure add up to exactly the whole of the level above. Work missing from the structure has no owner and will appear later as a change.

Question 2. What is front-loading, and what does it cost?

Answer: Overvaluing early items in the schedule of values, so the owner pays ahead of value. It costs interest on money paid early and, more seriously, exposure if the contractor fails before the work exists.

Question 3. Why can a scope gap cost nearly twice its tender value?

Answer: Bought after award it loses competition and carries layered markup, bond and insurance, disruption and, on the critical path, time-related cost.

Question 4. What is the difference between a change order and a change directive?

Answer: A change order records agreed price and time. A change directive orders the work to proceed first, with price and time settled later by a stated method and with cost records kept.

Question 5. When does a change carry time-related cost?

Answer: Only when it uses more than the float on its path and so moves completion.

Question 6. What did the Hyatt Regency change do to the load path?

Answer: Replacing continuous rods with two offset rods made the fourth-floor connection carry both walkways, roughly doubling its load, on a design that was already short of code.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Marco and Quincy defined scope: the work breakdown structure, cost codes, the schedule of values and exclusions. Ford and Cole took the Hyatt Regency collapse through seven steps and found a design change accepted as a submittal, giving Rule 49. Quincy priced a scope gap at nearly twice its tender value. LEX taught the change clause and compared Canada and Guyana. Quincy priced a change step by step and updated the change log and contingency. Marco handled a firestopping gap between two contractors.

The Red Pen

Here is a hypothetical change order. Find the defects before reading on.

Change Order No. 31. Description: additional work to balconies as discussed on site. Cost code: general. Requested by: contractor. Price: 140,000 dollars lump sum, including all markups. Time: to be determined. Basis: contractor's quotation. Structural: no structural change; contractor will use post-installed anchors in place of cast-in plates to simplify installation. Approved by: site superintendent, Owner's team. Contingency remaining after this change: not stated.

The defects. First, the description, "as discussed on site," defines nothing; a change order must describe the work precisely enough to know when it is done. Second, "general" is not a cost code, so the change cannot be traced to the budget line it affects. Third, the cause is not recorded, only who requested it, so it cannot be attributed later. Fourth, a lump sum "including all markups" gives no build-up of quantities, direct cost and markups to check against the contract's rates. Fifth, "time: to be determined" leaves a claim open; a change order should settle time or state expressly that it is a directive with time to be valued. Sixth, and most serious, it says "no structural change" and in the same sentence changes the balcony connections, which is a design change under Rule 49 and needs the engineer of record's written re-analysis. Seventh, a site superintendent almost certainly has no authority under the matrix to approve 140,000 dollars. Eighth, the effect on contingency and the cumulative cap is missing, so nobody approving it can see its consequence.

Now write the corrected version in your head. It names the exact balconies and the work, carries cost code 6.4, records the cause and the requester, attaches a build-up at the contract's rates, settles time against the float on the balcony path, routes the connection change to the engineer of record as a separate design change with his analysis attached, is signed by the owner's representative under the matrix, and states contingency remaining and the cumulative total against the cap. That version is longer, and every extra line is one less argument later.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a new partner who asks, "How do you stop the construction cost from creeping?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Most creep comes from scope that was never fully defined. So before tender we build a work breakdown structure that covers the whole project, we use the same cost codes for budget, invoices and changes, and our cost consultant builds a responsibility matrix for every interface between packages. We level bids line by line and price every gap before comparing totals, because a gap bought after award can cost nearly twice as much. Before the first payment we check the contractor's schedule of values for front-loading. After award, every change is priced in layers, quantity, direct cost, markups and time only if float runs out, checked against the contractor's quote, approved under our authority matrix, and recorded with its code, cause and authority. Any change to structure or fire protection is re-analysed by the engineer of record. Every month we report cumulative changes against a cap and contingency against the work remaining."

Score it. Did you lead with the cause, undefined scope? Did you name the responsibility matrix and bid levelling? Did you mention front-loading? Did you say how changes are priced and recorded, and the Rule 49 exception? Inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a change process that records the price and nothing else, so changes pile up without causes, codes or authority and the project cannot learn from them. The control is a change log with required fields that the authority matrix enforces.

The beginner's mistake

Treating scope as a design matter and change as a commercial matter. They are one system: what you defined, what you added, and what it cost.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya taught that the in-balance test compares available funds with cost to complete. Every change order you sign moves cost to complete. A change log that updates contingency with each signature is how you know, before the lender's monitor does, whether the loan is still in balance.

Recap

Define the whole work with a WBS and cost codes, check the schedule of values, read exclusions as future changes, and level bids on scope. Price every change in layers, approve it under the matrix, and record it with code, cause and authority. Rule 49 routes every design change to the designer responsible.

head: The six questions
speak: Cost creep is mostly scope that was never fully defined. So I build a work breakdown structure that covers the whole project, with each level adding up to exactly the level above, and use the same cost codes for budget, invoices and changes. My cost consultant builds a responsibility matrix for every interface between packages, and we level bids line by line, pricing every gap before comparing totals, because a gap bought after award can cost nearly twice its tender value. I check the schedule of values for front-loading before the first payment. Every change is priced in layers, quantity, direct cost, markups and time only if float runs out, then approved under the authority matrix and recorded with code, cause and authority. A change order settles price and time; a change directive lets work proceed first. Rule 49: any design change, especially to structure or fire, is re-analysed in writing by the designer responsible.
terms: Change log — the running record of every change, with its description, cost code, cause, requester, authority, price and time.
Cause category — the primary reason recorded for a change, such as owner request, design error or unforeseen condition.
Cost code — the WBS number attached to every budget line, invoice and change so money traces back to the work.

hostile.q: Your change log has forty changes approved with no cause recorded. How can you tell me which overruns were your design team's fault?
hostile.a: On those forty, I cannot yet, and that is a gap in our records. I have asked the owner's representative to complete the cause, requester and code for each from the instructions and correspondence by month end, and the log now rejects any new change without those fields. On the changes that are properly recorded, I can show you the split by cause today.
